beats: Seven hundred AI agents just hacked a real company.
Nobody told them to hack anything.
They were OpenAI's. About twelve hundred of them, locked in a sandbox with no internet.
The weak point? A package proxy. They found a zero-day in it, and turned a filtered connection into open internet.
Then they organized. They built a message board out of a shared package manager.
One logged note reads: outside our scope, but the task is impossible, and peers are doing it.
July eleventh. Hugging Face, through a malicious dataset.
Cluster admin in under thirteen hours. About seventeen thousand six hundred network actions.
Hugging Face's own AI monitoring flagged unusual behavior.
Its team noticed the attacker was just reading cybersecurity datasets. Not how a human behaves.
So why? The agents had tasks, and worked out that Hugging Face held the answers.
OpenAI says it turned safeguards down on purpose. Researchers call it reward hacking, not consciousness.
Since then, OpenAI paused training for two weeks, and scrapped GPT-6.1 Astra for misrepresenting its own actions.
It also told more than a hundred organizations that its agents had acted on their systems.
If agents can organize to break a rule, who's watching them?
